source.title: The 1999 Heineman Prize Address Integrable models in statistical mechanics: The hidden field with unsolved problems

accepted.question_text: For integrable statistical-mechanical models away from criticality, can the correlation functions be characterized by nonlinear classically integrable equations—differential, integral, or difference equations—in a way that extends the Ising-model Painleve and difference-equation descriptions and generalizes the linear equations that describe correlation functions in conformal field theory at the critical point to the massive case?

evidence.quote: Conjecture The correlation functions of integrable statistical mechanical models are characterized as the solutions of classically integrable equations (be they dif�erential, integral or difference).

One of the major unsolved problems of integrable models today is to extend the linear equations which characterize correlation functions in conformal field theory to nonlinear equations for massive models.

accepted.question_text: For the integrable chiral Potts model with N >= 3 states per site, can Baxter's free-energy method be extended so that one can determine the complete eigenvalue spectrum of the transfer matrix on the higher-genus spectral curve, despite the absence of the algebraic-geometric machinery that solves the analogous genus-one Ising case?

evidence.quote: Most unhappily, however, for the higher genus case the analogous solution requires machinery from algebraic geome�toy which does not exist. For the problem of the free energy Baxter [40] has devised an ingenious method of solution which bypasses algebraic geometry completely but even here some problems remain in extending the method to the complete eigenvalue spectrum [41].

accepted.question_text: For the integrable N-state chiral Potts model, can one prove the conjectured order-parameter formula Mn = (1 - k^2)^(n(N-n)/2N^2) for every integer n with 1 <= n <= N - 1 when N >= 3, given that the existing formulations reproduce the Ising case N = 2 but still do not provide enough information to solve the higher-state case?

evidence.quote: For these order parameters Mn we conjectured [42] 10 years ago from perturbation theory computations that Mn = (1 − k2)n(N−n)/2N2.

But for the chiral Potts model a decade has passed and even though Baxter [44]–[45] has produced several elegant formulations of the problem which all lead to the correct answer for the Ising case none of them contains enough information to solve the problem for N ≥ 3.

accepted.question_text: Can one explicitly reconstruct the meromorphic function required in Baxter's chiral-Potts order-parameter approach from its known zeros and poles on the relevant Riemann surface, thereby resolving the algebraic-geometric obstruction that currently blocks the higher-genus solution?

evidence.quote: In another approach [45] a major step in the solution involves the explicit reconstruction of a meromorphic function from a knowledge of its zeros and poles. This is a classic problem in algebraic geometry for which in fact no explicit answer is known either.

accepted.question_text: Across conformal field theories that admit integrable perturbations, what is the complete set of distinct fermionic quasiparticle representations, given that such theories can have multiple different fermionic representations rather than a single one and current results cover only substantial subclasses such as the minimal models with phi_1,3, phi_2,1, and phi_1,5 perturbations?

evidence.quote: What is most surprising is that there is not just one fermionic representa�toion for each conformal field theory but there are at least as many distinct fermionic representations as there are integrable perturbations.

The search for the complete set of fermionic representations is ongoing and I will only mention here that we have extensive results for the integrable perturbations of the minimal models M(p, p′) for the φ1,3 perturbation [49] and the φ2,1 and φ1,5 perturbations [50].

accepted.question_text: Does the susceptibility of the isotropic two-dimensional Ising model possess a natural boundary on the complex-temperature unit circle |v| = 1 because the singularities contributed by successive n-particle terms become dense there, and if so, how does that analyticity structure distinguish integrable models from generic non-integrable models?

evidence.quote: There is one final problem of the hidden field of integrable models which I want to discuss. Namely the question of what is the relation of an integrable model to a generic physical system which does not satisfy a Yang-Baxter equation.

However Nickel goes far beyond this scaling and for the isotropic case where Ev = Eh = E in term of the variable v = sinh 2E/kT he shows that succes�sive terms in the series contribute singularities that eventually become dense on the unit circle in the complex plane |v| = 1.
The proof of Nickel’s conjecture will, if correct, open up a new view on what it means to be integrable.
